persons.name: Stephen F. Gale
persons.note: Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named'. It gives a name, a trade and usually an arrival year, and it is a retrospective of 1884: a YEAR off it is documented, a MONTH is not, and it says nothing whatever about 1835. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Gale, Stephen F.” (poll_1833_011, line 32). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Gale' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Gale, Stephen F. | 1835, May, | Exeter, N. H. | 67 | Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json).

residents.research_note: THE ONLY MAN ON THE 1833 ROSTER GIVEN AN ORIGIN AND NO TRADE, which is the reverse of every other entry on it. He was one of the twenty-eight electors of 10 August 1833. A BOOKSELLER AND STATIONER IS A TRADE THIS DATASET WOULD LIKE TO CONFIRM: it would be the first evidence of a retail book trade in the town, and Andreas's chapter on bookbinders and stationers, which this parcel did not work, is where the confirmation would be.

persons.name: G. W. Keeney
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'G. W. KEENEY' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 7 May 1834, column 3. The corpus associates the name with Chicago; that is where the paper does business with this person and not a statement about where they slept, and the storefront tickets are the ones that may stand a shop there. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `founder` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry.

AN INITIAL THIS PROJECT CANNOT READ, MARKED AS ONE. The card shows 'A. [?] Perry': the scan sets a DIGIT where the middle initial goes, and a digit is never part of a name, so the character is carried as [?] — the marker the Chicago list of 1 January 1834 already uses for an initial the printing did not deliver. NO LETTER IS SUPPLIED. The deposit holds two transcriptions of this issue and no page image, and the alternate carries no letter list at all, so there is no cleaner impression here to settle it against and the project declines to guess (T-0721; the suspicion is registered, ungraded, at data/research/residents/letter_list_reading_suspicions.json). The verbatim setting is untouched and quoted above; what has stopped is the card asserting that setting is a name. A pass that reaches the page images settles it and this marker goes. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Abijah S. Perry” (f1839_v0646, printed page 45, ward 6, voting for John H. Kinzie). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Perry' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins A. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

persons.name: Giles Spring
persons.note: HIS FIRST OFFICE WAS A BARREL-HEAD AND HIS SECOND WAS DESK-ROOM IN CATON'S. The two of them opposed each other in the first larceny case heard before a justice of the peace in July 1833, and Caton's account of hiring out to carry the chain for a surveyor on the North Side that same month - because clients were few, fees small and board bills maturing - is the only description in this dataset of what an educated newcomer actually did for money in the town's first summer. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Spring, Giles” (poll_1834_103, line 272); Poll list of 1835 — “Spring, G.” (poll_1835_075, line 362). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Spring' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 3 times, as “SPRING GILES”, 1836-06-29 to 1836-09-05: 3 lots in the platted town — lot 4 of block 41 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L4BL41CHIOT, as printed); lot 5 of block 12 in the town the register codes CHIOTV (L5BL12CHIOTV, as printed); lot 6 of block 12 in the town the register codes CHIOTV (L6BL12CHIOTV, as printed), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $5850.00 (ls1465, ls1466, ls1467). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $5850.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: SPRING GILES matches Giles Spring: the forename names Giles Spring of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

what_it_supplies: A 665-roof production target with independently reconcilable group, district, level, and construction totals.

District character, spacing, variation, finish, and chronology constraints for a July 1835 reconstruction.

what_it_does_not_supply: A surviving July 1835 building census or parcel-by-parcel roof register.
Exact locations, dimensions, appearance, occupants, or construction dates for anonymous roofs.
Authority to replace stronger building-specific evidence already represented in the dataset.
